job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a master's in environmental engineering in Houston, finishing my first year. I live with my parents in Pasadena, Texas, and drive forty minutes to campus. Mornings I'm in water-treatment lectures, afternoons I'm in the lab, and Wednesdays I sit in on my father's construction firm's bid meetings. My fiancé Daniel and I are getting married next June at our church, so a lot of evenings go to venue and budget talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a tool, like the calculator was, and that it'll find its place. At church I'd say what matters is how people treat each other, not what machines can do. At the lab I'd say nothing and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is the good outcome. Water plants and pipes need engineers, Daniel's job as a high-school coach is safe, and our wedding budget works. I use AI now and then to double-check my math, and I'm fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a job at the city's water department and keep helping my father with his bids. Daniel and I would marry in June and rent a small house near my parents. I'd keep a few thousand dollars aside for emergencies and keep paying into our wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good. A bit like a deep breath. I don't want my wedding year to be a year of panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like more young people to see engineering as service. Clean water is a calling, honestly. In a plateau, I could do twenty good years of that without watching my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there pressures you carry anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cost of the wedding, mostly, and my father's firm. Steel and lumber prices keep going up, and he's told me he might not bid on two city jobs this year. I'm trying to help him, but I'm not the owner.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool**, like the calculator was, and it'll find its place.
At church I'd say what matters is how **people treat each other**.
think: A plateau is the **good outcome** because water plants and pipes need engineers.
Daniel's job as a **coach** is safe and our wedding budget works.
do: Finish the master's and take a job at the city **water department**.
Keep helping my father with his **bids** and marry Daniel in June.
feel: I feel **good**, like a deep breath, because I don't want a wedding year of panic.
S0.quote: Clean water is a calling, honestly. In a plateau, I could do twenty good years of that without watching my back.
fieldNote: Maya is **secure** and sees engineering as a calling.
The household pressure is her father's firm and rising material costs.
Faith and the wedding anchor her priorities.

steps.text: Take a job at the city water department after graduating
Keep helping my father write bids on Wednesdays
Keep a few thousand dollars aside as an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep our heads. The change is serious, but families and churches have survived worse. I'd tell friends to save and learn something practical. And I'd tell my father that his bid paperwork will go to software sooner or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy. Calculations, reports and permit forms are exactly the thinking tasks AI takes. The city might hire fewer juniors and use software for compliance. Daniel's coaching job is safe, but ours is a one-and-a-half-income household for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools at work now, not just once in a while, so I can tell good output from bad. I'd take a water-quality certification, which needs an engineer's signature. I'd also push the wedding budget down by a few thousand and keep more in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a rain cloud that you can see but can't tell when it will arrive. I'm not panicking, but I carry an umbrella.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer guests, from a hundred and eighty to a hundred and twenty. Daniel's mother would be hurt, but she'd get over it. I'd rather start our marriage with room in the bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father about his firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to digitise the estimates and use an AI tool to check them for missed items. He'll grumble that he's done it by hand for thirty years. But thirty years of experience plus a checker beats experience alone. I'd tell him so kindly.

say: I'd say we should **keep our heads**, since families and churches have survived worse.
I'd tell my father his **bid paperwork** will go to software sooner or later.
think: Calculations, reports and permit forms are the **thinking tasks** AI takes first.
The city might hire fewer **juniors** and use software for compliance.
do: Use AI tools at work **daily** to tell good output from bad and take a water-quality certification.
Cut the wedding budget by a few **thousand** and keep more in savings.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like seeing a rain cloud and carrying an umbrella.
S1.quote: Thirty years of experience plus a checker beats experience alone.
fieldNote: Maya is **uneasy** and acts through certification and a leaner wedding.
She tries to help her father modernise without insulting his experience.
Her fiancé's steady job reduces household risk.

steps.text: Use AI tools at work daily to learn their mistakes
Earn a water quality engineer certification within a year
Cut wedding guests from 180 to 120 and save the difference
Show my father how to check bids with an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a flood. I'd say the government should not mandate anything, but it should not leave families holding the bill either. I'd tell people at church to look after each other and share what they have. And I'd tell Daniel that we can still marry, but small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 the thinking work in engineering goes, and I'd be 26 with a master's and a wedding behind me. The hands-on robots come around 2031, which leaves water plants and field crews safer for a while, but city budgets might shrink if tax income falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a field-heavy job at a utility instead of a design role, and I'd keep my father's firm going with every hour I have. We'd marry at the church hall rather than the venue and save the deposit. I'd also ask our pastor about the church's help fund, though I'd hate to need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like someone has shifted the ground right as I was about to step. I'm scared, but I also feel stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we make a plan together and don't hide numbers from each other. His coaching job doesn't depend on AI, and that's a relief. But he knows that if my income dips we'd need to move in with my parents for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies, and the people who cheered them on without asking about families. I'm not for banning anything, but speed without responsibility isn't progress. If you break something, you help fix it.

say: I'd say the government shouldn't mandate anything but must not leave **families holding the bill**.
I'd tell people at church to **look after each other**.
think: By 2028 the thinking work in engineering goes, and I'd be **26** with a master's and a wedding behind me.
City **budgets** might shrink if tax income falls.
do: Take a **field-heavy** utility job and keep my father's firm going with every spare hour.
Hold the wedding in the **church hall** and save the venue deposit.
feel: I feel **scared** but stubborn, as if the ground shifted just as I stepped.
S2.quote: Speed without responsibility isn't progress. If you break something, you help fix it.
fieldNote: Maya is **anxious** and leans on faith, family and a wedding downsize.
She is clear about her fiancé's stable job but admits a fallback of living with parents.
Her blame is for speed without responsibility, not for technology.

steps.text: Take a field-heavy utility job instead of a design role
Move the wedding from the venue to the church hall
Ask our pastor about the church's help fund as a backup
Work extra hours on my father's firm bids

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a decent stretch. I'd say we need to teach people to adapt, and that churches and neighbours can help with that. I'd say it calmly because I want to be someone who steadies others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy but hopeful. By 2031 I'd be 29, perhaps with a child, and ready for a field leadership job. The thinking work goes by then, but the pipes and plants need people until the robots reach them around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a water utility as a field engineer, then move into operations. I'd use AI tools for reports, and I'd train staff on safe use. Daniel and I would buy a house, and I'd keep paying into a rainy-day fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like preparing for a long drive. Fill the tank, check the map, call mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your father's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help him modernise with estimating software and then think about joining him. I'd rather stay an engineer than become a boss, but I'd do it if the firm needed me. We have a few good people there who'd be hurt if it closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small group that teaches older people how to use these tools safely. I know a retired teacher who'd run it. People my grandparents' age will get scammed otherwise.

say: I'd say we need to **teach people to adapt**, and churches and neighbours can help.
I'd say it **calmly**, because I want to steady others.
think: By 2031 I'd be 29, perhaps with a child, and ready for a **field leadership** job.
Pipes and plants need people until robots reach them around **2034**.
do: Work as a **field engineer** at a water utility, then move into operations.
Buy a **house** with Daniel and keep a rainy-day fund.
feel: I feel **hopeful** but uneasy, like preparing for a long drive.
S3.quote: People my grandparents' age will get scammed otherwise.
fieldNote: Maya's plan is **field and operations**, with family and church woven in.
She sees a community role for older people's tech safety.
Her loyalty to her father's firm competes with her engineering path.

steps.text: Work as a field engineer at a water utility
Start a church group on safe technology for older people
Buy a house with Daniel and keep a rainy-day fund
Use AI tools for reports and train colleagues on safe use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the version where good people can make good plans. I'd say we should pass rules slowly and give workers training time. I'd also say we should teach young people trades and values at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd be 34 with years of field experience, probably with two children and a lead role. The hands-on robots come around 2039, which feels far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in water, rise to project engineer, and help my father decide whether to sell or hand over the firm. I'd learn AI tools slowly and make sure they're safe for drinking-water decisions. Daniel and I would buy a house near the church and have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels warm. A long time to build a family and a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to people who feel it's all happening too fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That ten years is enough if we use it, and that nobody has to do it alone. At church we say bear one another's burdens. I'd like my engineering to do some of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'd put my career above everything and missed my kids' school plays. A world with more time could mean more time at home, and I'd like to be ready for that.

say: I'd say we should pass rules **slowly** and give workers training time.
I'd teach young people **trades and values** together.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 with years of **field experience** and a lead role.
The hands-on robots come around 2039, which feels **far off**.
do: Rise to **project engineer** and help my father decide whether to sell or hand over the firm.
Buy a **house** near the church and have children.
feel: I feel **warm**, with a long time to build a family and a career.
S4.quote: At church we say bear one another's burdens. I'd like my engineering to do some of that.
fieldNote: Maya's ten-year picture is **family-centred** and faith-guided.
She wants her engineering to carry the idea of bearing one another's burdens.
She is willing to let the family firm go if it makes sense.

steps.text: Rise to project engineer in a water utility

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be starting a marriage and a career in the same year with the ground shifting. What would help is time for small firms to adapt, and neighbours who look out for each other. I'd also want the companies to carry some of the cost when they cause disruption.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people think faith and technology are at odds, but I don't. The question is whether we use new things to look after each other, and that's the question I try to ask.

headlineQuote: The question is whether we use new things to look after each other, and that's the question I try to ask.
portrait: Maya is 24, doing an **environmental engineering** master's in Houston and living with her parents in Pasadena, Texas.
She uses AI now and then and values faith, family and **community help** in all her plans.
Her traditional outlook favours work, neighbours and family support over handouts.
She is marrying Daniel next June, so her **wedding and budget** shape her choices in every scenario.
Her father's construction firm adds a household worry and a possible **duty** in future.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she'd be starting a marriage and a career in the same year with the ground shifting.
whatWouldHelp: **Time for small firms** to adapt, neighbours who look out for each other and companies carrying some of the cost.
